accordions.heading: What is HIV?
accordions.content:
HIV is a virus that affects the immune system. It can be passed on through sex without a condom and may cause no noticeable symptoms for a long time.

There is currently no cure for HIV, but treatment is highly effective and allows people living with HIV to live long, healthy lives.

accordions.heading: Is this for you?
accordions.content:
You don’t need to have symptoms to test. HIV can cause no noticeable symptoms.

It may be worth testing if:
accordions.after: Had a possible HIV exposure in the last 72 hours? Don’t wait for a test result. Contact a sexual health clinic or go to A&E as soon as possible and ask about PEP, medication that can help prevent HIV after exposure.
checklist: You have a new sexual partner or more than one partner
A sexual partner has told you they have HIV or another STI
You have possible symptoms, such as a flu-like illness

benefits.text: Everything you need to test for HIV at home:

how.heading: How does the test work?
how.intro:
The test looks for antibodies your body can produce in response to HIV-1 or HIV-2 infection, using a small finger-prick blood sample.

Your result appears on the test pad in around 15 minutes, with no sample to send to a laboratory.

steps.title: Prick your finger
steps.text: Wash your hands and clean your fingertip with an alcohol pad. Let it dry, then use the lancet to prick your finger and form a drop of blood.

steps.title: Add blood and diluent
steps.text: Use the pipette to collect your blood and add 1 drop to the sample well marked S on the test pad. Then add 4 drops of diluent (test liquid) to the same well, immediately after the blood.

steps.title: Read your result
steps.text: Leave the test pad flat and read your result between 15 and 20 minutes. Don't read the test after 20 minutes, as the result may no longer be reliable.

windows.heading: When should I test?
windows.subheading: Testing too early can give a negative result even if you have an infection.

questions.question: When should I take an HIV test?
questions.answer:
You can test at any time, but the window period matters. A negative result from an antibody-only rapid test may need repeating if the exposure was within the last 90 days.

You don't need to have symptoms to test for HIV. Testing is recommended if you think you may have been exposed, have a new sexual partner or want to check your HIV status.

questions.question: How soon after sex can I test for HIV?
questions.answer:
You can test straight away, but a test taken very soon after exposure may not detect a new HIV infection.

For this antibody-only rapid test, use a 90-day window period. If your result is negative before then, repeat testing after 90 days may be needed.

A sexual health clinic can offer tests that detect HIV earlier.

questions.question: It’s been less than 72 hours since I may have been exposed to HIV. What should I do?
questions.answer:
Contact a sexual health clinic or go to A&E as soon as possible and ask about PEP (post-exposure prophylaxis).

PEP is medication that can help prevent HIV after exposure. It must be started within 72 hours and works best when started as soon as possible.

questions.question: How reliable is this HIV rapid test?
questions.answer:
When used correctly, this test provides a reliable way to check for HIV antibodies at home.

Testing too soon after exposure can affect your result, so an early negative may need to be repeated. This is a screening test, so a positive result should be followed up with a sexual health clinic for further testing.

questions.question: What does a negative HIV test result mean?
questions.answer:
A negative result means no HIV antibodies were detected.

HIV can take time to show up on a test. If you may have been exposed within the last 90 days, test again at least 90 days after your last possible exposure.

If you have symptoms or are concerned, contact a sexual health clinic for advice about testing sooner.

questions.question: What if my result is positive?
questions.answer: A positive result doesn't necessarily mean you have HIV. You'll need another test to confirm it. Contact a sexual health clinic as soon as possible and let them know you've had a positive rapid HIV test. If HIV is confirmed, effective treatment is available. People living with HIV can live long, healthy lives. NHS sexual health services are free and confidential. If HIV is confirmed, the clinic can also advise you about informing sexual partners.

questions.question: Can I take an HIV test while pregnant?
questions.answer:
If you're pregnant and concerned about HIV, speak to your midwife, GP or a sexual health clinic.

HIV testing is routinely offered during pregnancy through the NHS. Early diagnosis and treatment can help protect both you and your baby.
